  <title>Win for Washington as judge blocks unlawful federal implementation of Medicaid work requirements</title>
  <link>https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/win-washington-judge-blocks-unlawful-federal-implementation-medicaid-work</link>
  <description>
<span>Win for Washington as judge blocks&nbsp;unlawful federal implementation of Medicaid work requirements</span>

  <div class="bottom-padded">
    <div class="field-label"> FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:</div>
              <div><time datetime="2026-10-29T14:52:24-07:00">Oct 29 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>

<span><span lang about="https://www.atg.wa.gov/users/atgsamblobaum" typeof="schema:Person" property="schema:name" datatype>atgSamBlobaum</span></span>

<span><time datetime="2026-10-29T14:51:15-07:00" title="Thursday, October 29, 2026 - 14:51">Thu, 10/29/2026 - 14:51</time>
</span>

            <div><p>A judge blocked the federal government’s unlawful implementation of new Medicaid work requirements that would have made it even harder for people with challenging medical conditions to get the healthcare they need, delivering a victory to Washington and a multistate coalition that brought the case in <a href="https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/ag-brown-sues-over-unlawful-federal-implementation-medicaid-work-requirements">June 2026</a>.</p>
<p>The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts found the administration’s implementation of new Medicaid work requirements under the Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1) was unlawful. The rule adopted a new interpretation of key terms like “medically frail,”&nbsp;making it harder for medically vulnerable individuals to be excused from the work requirements.&nbsp;</p>
<p>“Our state is healthier, safer, and more productive when everyone can get the care they need,” said Attorney General Nick Brown. “We will continue to defend Medicaid as the federal government uses bureaucracy and red tape to try to deny Washingtonians the care they deserve.”</p>
<p>Medicaid is the nation’s safety net healthcare program for low-income Americans. Congress created exemptions from Medicaid’s work requirements to ensure that people with serious illnesses and disabilities do not lose coverage or face interruptions in care. Apple Health is Washington’s Medicaid program and insures approximately 1.9 million individuals, including some of the most vulnerable people in the state, such as those experiencing homelessness or who have serious or complex medical conditions.</p>
<p>Despite months of working with states on implementation, CMS surprised states with the interim final rule, “Community Engagement Requirement for Certain Individuals” in June 2026.&nbsp;</p>
<p>Past Medicaid work requirement programs have shown that rules that add red tape like the June 2026 rule cause eligible people to lose coverage, place greater strain on state Medicaid programs, safety net providers, and emergency rooms, while increasing costs as more medically frail residents become uninsured.&nbsp;</p>
<p>In today’s decision, the District Court held that the Trump Administration’s definition of “medical frailty” is contrary to law, vacated the language, issued a permanent injunction, and granted the plaintiff states’ a six-month stay of enforcement to accommodate any errors or delays resulting from the necessary changes to implementation.&nbsp;</p>
<p><a href="https://agportal-s3bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Federal%20Litigation/dkt%20147%20opinion%20on%20MSJ.pdf?VersionId=7vreJGlptF.J.OUItCICZphx0K0bYc.7">Read the decision.</a></p>

  <title>GM to pay $220M for sharing drivers’ private data in case co-led by Washington</title>
  <link>https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/gm-pay-220m-sharing-drivers-private-data-case-co-led-washington</link>
  <description>
<span>GM to pay $220M for sharing drivers’ private data in case co-led by Washington</span>

  <div class="bottom-padded">
    <div class="field-label"> FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:</div>
              <div><time datetime="2026-10-29T09:28:29-07:00">Oct 29 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>

<span><span lang about="https://www.atg.wa.gov/users/atgsamblobaum" typeof="schema:Person" property="schema:name" datatype>atgSamBlobaum</span></span>

<span><time datetime="2026-10-29T09:27:10-07:00" title="Thursday, October 29, 2026 - 09:27">Thu, 10/29/2026 - 09:27</time>
</span>

            <div><p>General Motors will pay $220 million to settle <a href="https://agportal-s3bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Consumer%20Protection/GM_Complaint.pdf?VersionId=pri7OJSF1W0rrL30NaMiGy8bP.1leGDp">allegations</a> that it illegally sold consumers’ private driver behavior data and location information to third parties, including data brokers, who then sold the data to insurance companies. For many consumers, this data was used by insurance companies in part to set insurance rates.&nbsp;</p>
<p>Washington co-led a coalition of 36 attorneys general in the case against GM, and the state will receive $12.3 million through the settlement. The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative express consent from consumers before collecting or disclosing consumer driving and location data.&nbsp;</p>
<p>“Washingtonians’ data is personal and valuable, which is why they should always have control over how it’s used,” said Attorney General Nick Brown. “We’re proud to lead this bipartisan agreement holding GM accountable for misusing drivers’ data.”&nbsp;</p>
<p>From 2016 to 2024, GM enrolled millions of drivers in their Smart Driver program, which tracked their driving habits. GM pitched this tool as a way for drivers to improve their own driving safety and told drivers that they would not share their data with insurers without express consent.</p>
<p>However, the AG’s investigation found that GM sold this information to data brokers under contracts that specified the data was to be used for insurance products. The data brokers sold the data to insurance companies, who could then change the driver’s premium based on their driving habits. GM did not disclose to drivers that their data would be sold for this purpose.&nbsp;</p>
<p>Most customers who signed up for Smart Driver did so at the GM dealership when they bought their car. GM used one sign-up process for drivers to enroll in Smart Driver along with GM’s OnStar services. In many cases, dealership employees allegedly accepted terms and conditions on behalf of customers without their consent. At the time, GM was heavily incentivizing dealerships to sign up as many customers for OnStar as possible. Sales employees received bonuses based in part on how many customers signed up for GM’s connected vehicle services and dealerships were ranked based on their enrollment numbers.</p>
<p>GM’s own systems failed to notify drivers about whether their data was being tracked. The OnStar app mistakenly told over 370,000 drivers that they were not enrolled in Smart Driver, when they actually were enrolled and GM was collecting and selling their data. GM later quietly unenrolled these over 370,000 drivers without telling them about the mistake and left their data with the data brokers and insurance companies.&nbsp;</p>
<p>The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific. Insurers had data showing how many times a person drove their vehicle, the start and end times of each drive, how many times they braked or accelerated quickly, and whether they went faster than the speed limit. As documented in the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/11/technology/carmakers-driver-tracking-insurance.html">New York Times</a>, insurance companies then used this information to change rates, sometimes increasing their premiums. After the Times reported on these practices, GM discontinued the Smart Driver program.</p>
<p>The settlement also requires GM to limit the driving data it collects from consumers and protect their personal information going forward as part of a comprehensive data privacy program. The terms secured by Washington and the coalition are significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct including by mandating internal and external data protection and privacy program assessments. GM also agreed to oversight and training requirements at their dealerships to protect consumers against being enrolled in data collection schemes without their consent.</p>
<p>AGO attorneys and staff who worked on this case include Assistant Attorneys General Katy Box, Andrea Alegrett, and Bret Finkelstein, and paralegals Judy Lim and Michelle Paules.</p>
<p>The case was co-led by Washington and Oregon, assisted by the Executive Committee of Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Kentucky, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, Utah, and Vermont, and joined by the attorneys general of Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, the District Of Columbia, Florida, Hawai’i, Idaho, Kansas, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Virginia, and Wisconsin.</p>
<p><a href="https://agportal-s3bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Consumer%20Protection/2026_10_29ConsentDecree.pdf?VersionId=tk7im_GjEEbD1gSHW4qitoLjQ_0Y4HIK">Read the consent decree.</a></p>

  <title>AG Brown sues to block the federal administration’s gutting of the Corporate Transparency Act</title>
  <link>https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/ag-brown-sues-block-federal-administration-s-gutting-corporate-transparency-act</link>
  <description>
<span>AG Brown sues to block the federal administration’s gutting of the Corporate Transparency Act</span>

  <div class="bottom-padded">
    <div class="field-label"> FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:</div>
              <div><time datetime="2026-10-27T12:23:00-07:00">Oct 27 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>

<span><span lang about="https://www.atg.wa.gov/users/atgashleygross" typeof="schema:Person" property="schema:name" datatype>atgAshleyGross</span></span>

<span><time datetime="2026-10-27T12:22:43-07:00" title="Tuesday, October 27, 2026 - 12:22">Tue, 10/27/2026 - 12:22</time>
</span>

            <div><p>Attorney General Nick Brown has joined a coalition of 20 states in a lawsuit to stop the federal administration from gutting a law that helps banking regulators and law enforcement investigate shell companies and crack down on financial crime.</p>
<p>The law, the Corporate Transparency Act, requires corporations and limited liability companies to disclose to the federal government who actually owns and controls them. That matters because criminals often hide their money in shell companies—entities that exist on paper to obscure a company’s ownership. Now the United States Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, known as FinCEN, has exempted 99.9% of corporations from the law, making it nearly useless.</p>
<p>“The administration is sending a loud message to financial criminals that the federal government doesn’t care what they do,” Brown said. “Our office will fight this unlawful attempt to let corporations hide assets, dodge taxes, and evade scrutiny.”</p>
<p>Congress passed the Corporate Transparency Act with bipartisan support in 2021. It created a Treasury database of owners of corporate entities that law enforcement can use to trace dirty money, track down stolen assets, and uncover bribes and political payoffs.</p>
<p>In August 2026, the Trump administration issued a rule exempting nearly every corporation from reporting. Then FinCEN went further, announcing it would delete the ownership information already in the database, records that likely include evidence of unsolved crimes. The states argue that would break multiple federal laws.</p>
<p>The lawsuit says FinCEN:</p>
<ul>
<li data-list-item-id="ec54ae4fef4f79f450a337a518c61a408">Violated the Corporate Transparency Act and Administrative Procedure Act.</li>
<li data-list-item-id="e8d65e9e127ad51670dc4211b75039666">Skipped required legal steps before changing the rule.</li>
<li data-list-item-id="e30fbb355ad0bb787c02724adf42b9cae">Acted arbitrarily and without a reasonable explanation.</li>
<li data-list-item-id="e16170319ed073dfb8b4ebfbea43f8c5a">Failed to properly consult the Secretary of Homeland Security and the U.S. Attorney General before exempting nearly all businesses.</li>
</ul>
<p>&nbsp;If the states win, the court would throw out FinCEN’s rule and require the agency to keep collecting and maintaining the ownership database for law enforcement.</p>
<p>The case, <em>State of Oregon v. Bessent</em>, is being filed today in U.S. District Court in Eugene.</p>
<p>The case is led by Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul. In addition to Brown, the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Washington, DC, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Virginia, and Wisconsin joined the lawsuit.</p>
<p><a href="https://agportal-s3bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Federal%20Litigation/FinCEN%20Rule%20Complaint%201%2010.27.26.pdf?VersionId=UKbuEgGtwyt4coMzB0BW0XKchO3D5KTD">Read the complaint</a>.</p>

  <title>AG’s Office finalizes model Public Records Act rules to improve transparency</title>
  <link>https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/ag-s-office-finalizes-model-public-records-act-rules-improve-transparency</link>
  <description>
<span>AG’s Office finalizes model Public Records Act rules to improve transparency</span>

  <div class="bottom-padded">
    <div class="field-label"> FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:</div>
              <div><time datetime="2026-10-27T09:34:02-07:00">Oct 27 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>

<span><span lang about="https://www.atg.wa.gov/users/atgashleygross" typeof="schema:Person" property="schema:name" datatype>atgAshleyGross</span></span>

<span><time datetime="2026-10-27T09:33:17-07:00" title="Tuesday, October 27, 2026 - 09:33">Tue, 10/27/2026 - 09:33</time>
</span>

            <div><p>The Attorney General’s Office (AGO) has released new model rules for government agencies to comply with the Public Records Act, incorporating feedback from hundreds of oral and written public comments about the AG’s proposed rules over the last year.<br>&nbsp;<br>“This update reduces barriers to information for the public and encourages government agencies to be proactive about transparency, both to better serve their constituents and to stay in compliance with the Public Records Act,” Attorney General Nick Brown said. “Our public records laws reflect the high standards Washingtonians hold their public servants to, and these new model rules honor those expectations.”<br>&nbsp;<br>The process of&nbsp;<a href="https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/ag-brown-proposes-model-public-records-act-rules-improve-government-transparency">developing new model rules</a>&nbsp;was initiated in 2025 by a rulemaking petition from news organizations concerned about increases in the time for responses to requests under the state’s Public Records Act.&nbsp;<br>&nbsp;<br>The AGO filed an initial proposal to revise the Model Rules and held a public hearing in November 2025. After public comment and testimony on the initial proposal, the AGO proposed revisions to some sections of the model rules for further public comment. A second public hearing to consider comments on the revised rules was held in June 2026. &nbsp;&nbsp;<br>&nbsp;<br>The new rules filed with the state Code Revisor reflect recent court decisions and provide clarity on submitting a records request, records production in a timely manner, and third-party notice of records requests. They also include updates for internal consistency and to address copy edit errors, among other amendments.<br>&nbsp;<br>A copy of the final rules and associated documents are available on the&nbsp;<a href="https://www.atg.wa.gov/rulemaking-activity">AGO website</a>, including a summary of all comments received and the AGO’s response to those comments.&nbsp;<br>&nbsp;<br>The final model rules encourage agencies to:</p>
<ul>
<li data-list-item-id="ece20c33b1f53eaf81b04016173004ab0">Triage requests into simple and complex tracks to ensure that processing times are proportionate to the difficulty of each request.</li>
<li data-list-item-id="ee90cc7e8b0e84e9206593cb3a93ffd6e">Provide records with their initial five-day response where the request is for a single, specific, readily available identifiable record.</li>
<li data-list-item-id="e3305c4a61dd115ad6b17a2eee34db7a6">Make sure the agency has a reasonable belief that the records are arguably exempt from disclosure before issuing a third-party notice.</li>
</ul>
<p>The model rules also say agencies should:</p>
<ul>
<li data-list-item-id="ed0506f778c564920ba91363d7b027d2b">Address the need to make public records accessible for search and production.</li>
<li data-list-item-id="e1194047db14654e3e7806deb4037c5b8">Send requesters a closure letter, consistent with court precedent, to let them know when an agency is no longer working on a response and the one-year timeframe for judicial review has begun.</li>
</ul>
<p>The AGO provides model rules that public agencies at any level of government across the state can adopt, in whole or in part, as part of its work to help agencies meet their legal obligations under the Public Records Act.<br>&nbsp;<br>Washington’s&nbsp;<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=42.56">Public Records Act</a>, which originally passed as a ballot initiative in 1972, is designed to prioritize transparency in government. It states “the people of this state do not yield their sovereignty to the agencies that serve them. The people, in delegating authority, do not give their public servants the right to decide what is good for the people to know and what is not good for them to know.”</p>
<p class="text-align-center">-30-</p>

As the state’s largest law firm, the Attorney General’s Office provides legal representation to every state agency, board, and commission in Washington. Additionally, the Office serves the people directly by enforcing consumer protection, civil rights, and environmental protection laws. The Office also prosecutes elder abuse, Medicaid fraud, and handles sexually violent predator cases in 38 of Washington’s 39 counties. <item>
  <title>AG’s office defends workers’ right to moonlight in settlement with Kiddie Academy</title>
  <link>https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/ag-s-office-defends-workers-right-moonlight-settlement-kiddie-academy</link>
  <description>
<span>AG’s office defends workers’ right to moonlight in settlement with Kiddie Academy</span>

  <div class="bottom-padded">
    <div class="field-label"> FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:</div>
              <div><time datetime="2026-10-23T12:55:20-07:00">Oct 23 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>

<span><span lang about="https://www.atg.wa.gov/users/atgsamblobaum" typeof="schema:Person" property="schema:name" datatype>atgSamBlobaum</span></span>

<span><time datetime="2026-10-23T12:50:09-07:00" title="Friday, October 23, 2026 - 12:50">Fri, 10/23/2026 - 12:50</time>
</span>

            <div><p>The Attorney General’s Office entered a <a href="https://agportal-s3bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Worker%20Rights%20Unit/006_GrantedConsentDecree.pdf?VersionId=5WudkuuCRNy5YfDnkwy9pdQd0Hyt7WiN">consent decree</a> today with seven Kiddie Academy childcare centers resolving <a href="https://agportal-s3bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Worker%20Rights%20Unit/002_Complaint.pdf?VersionId=vIctNJK3xE3XcHIaSu8q7jwZpY7sJCGY">claims</a> they illegally prevented employees from working other jobs in their off hours. Under Washington law, employers can’t restrict workers’ ability to work a second job or work as an independent contractor if they are paying those workers less than twice the hourly minimum wage. Employment restrictions can keep workers in jobs they would prefer to leave, and outside employment can provide additional income and new opportunities.</p>
<p>Under the terms of the settlement, the childcare centers will pay $252,500 to the affected workers and reform their policies. This is the first case resolved by Attorney General Nick Brown’s Worker Rights Unit established in November 2025.</p>
<p>“Our economy has delivered incredible prosperity to some Washingtonians, but workers are facing rising prices and fewer opportunities,” said AG Nick Brown. “Our Worker Rights Unit was created to support workers and enforce labor protections, and that’s exactly what we did in this case. We will continue to hold employers accountable when they break Washington law.”</p>
<p>Kiddie Academy is a nationwide childcare company that operates in a franchise model. The seven childcare centers included in this consent decree are all related franchises, Seattle Academy LLC, Bellevue Childcare LLC, Bothell Academy LLC, Greenwood Academy LLC, Kenmore Academy LLC, Mill Creek Academy LLC, and Redkirk Academy LLC, which are in King and Snohomish counties.</p>
<p>The AG’s office received complaints from childcare center workers that their employer restricted them from providing childcare services outside work hours to families who were currently or formerly enrolled at the school. The AG’s office alleges that prohibiting employees from taking outside employment or working as independent contractors is a clear violation of Washington <a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=49.62.070">law</a>. The office also alleges the company’s policies included non-disparagement clauses that did not include whistleblower protections required by <a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=49.44.211">law</a>.&nbsp;</p>
<p>The settlement requires the childcare centers to pay $252,500 to workers who were harmed by the illegal policies. The AG’s office estimates more than 600 workers may have been impacted, since the policies were companywide. The childcare centers must distribute the fund and report the settlement payments made to the AG’s office.&nbsp;</p>
<p>The childcare centers must also change their policies so that employees are not restricted from obtaining outside work and that their non-disparagement clause includes whistleblower protections. The AG’s office will monitor their compliance for the next two years.&nbsp;</p>
<p>AGO attorneys and staff who worked on this case include Assistant Attorney General Mark Rose and Paralegal Victoria Barbaglia.</p>
<p>In 2027, the <a href="https://www.lni.wa.gov/workers-rights/wages/minimum-wage/">minimum wage</a> in Washington will be $17.73 an hour for most workers. The law that guarantees workers’ ability to seek outside employment will apply to workers making less than $35.46 an hour in much of the state, though that number will be higher for workers in localities with a higher minimum wage.&nbsp;</p>
<p>Washington workers who believe their rights have been violated can contact the <a href="mailto:WorkerRights@atg.wa.gov">Worker Rights Unit</a>.</p>
<p><a href="https://agportal-s3bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Worker%20Rights%20Unit/006_GrantedConsentDecree.pdf?VersionId=5WudkuuCRNy5YfDnkwy9pdQd0Hyt7WiN">Read the consent decree.</a></p>

  <title>Washington’s police use-of-force dashboard delivers transparency to the public</title>
  <link>https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/washington-s-police-use-force-dashboard-delivers-transparency-public</link>
  <description>
<span>Washington’s police use-of-force dashboard delivers transparency to the public</span>

  <div class="bottom-padded">
    <div class="field-label"> FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:</div>
              <div><time datetime="2026-10-23T10:05:14-07:00">Oct 23 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>

<span><span lang about="https://www.atg.wa.gov/users/atgashleygross" typeof="schema:Person" property="schema:name" datatype>atgAshleyGross</span></span>

<span><time datetime="2026-10-23T10:04:50-07:00" title="Friday, October 23, 2026 - 10:04">Fri, 10/23/2026 - 10:04</time>
</span>

            <div><p>The Attorney General’s Office held a “Data, Transparency, and Police Use of Force” community forum in Everett Thursday evening to advance the office’s transparency work, partnership with local law enforcement, and commitment to community engagement.&nbsp;</p>
<p>The public safety event featured a presentation on the Washington State Data Exchange for Public Safety (<a href="https://wadeps.org/home/dashboard/">WADEPS</a>), which makes police use-of-force data available to everyone in the state. The evening also featured a panel discussion with community members and law enforcement, as well as a question-and-answer period with members of the public.&nbsp;</p>
<p>“Transparency and access to information are essential to building trust. This data tool empowers the public, policymakers, and law enforcement agencies to better understand interactions between the police and the community and make informed decisions about policing practices,” Brown said. “Our partnership with law enforcement agencies across the state is key to delivering this vital information to Washingtonians.”</p>
<p>“Public data dashboards provide a much-needed window into the trends and contributing factors surrounding the use of force by police. As more and more data is added, WADEPS has the potential to become&nbsp;a powerful tool that the public, policymakers, and law enforcement agencies can use collectively to improve transparency and affect positive outcomes for public safety in Washington state,” said&nbsp;David&nbsp;Makin, a criminal justice researcher at Washington State University and program director for WADEPS.</p>
<p>"Transparency in policing is the foundation upon which public trust is built. By providing a comprehensive, streamlined, and publicly available database, WADEPs serves to ensure efficient accessibility to use-of-force data and improves transparency between law enforcement agencies and the communities they serve,” said Chief Robert Goetz, Everett Police Department. “Moving forward, WADEPs will help agencies across the state make evidence-based policy decisions and continue to prioritize safety for all.”</p>
<p>“Trust has to be earned through a process people can examine. I appreciate WADEPS and everyone building it. We strengthen that investment by making sure every required incident is reported, identifying where information came from, and checking it against other evidence,” said Nickeia Hunter, Washington Coalition for Police Accountability. “The answer to skepticism is verification: show what is known, what remains disputed, what is missing, and who is responsible for resolving it.”</p>
<p>Since WADEPS went live in September 2025, the dashboard has recorded more than 4 million calls for service to law enforcement agencies across the state and more than 1,800 reportable uses of force. Agencies have up to 30 days after an incident to submit the required data to WADEPS. Washington State University developed WADEPS for the Attorney General’s Office and continues to manage it, standardizing reporting across hundreds of law enforcement agencies to allow the public to easily compare police use of force across the state.</p>
<p>Visitors to the dashboard can examine police rates of force across different types of calls for service, such as an assault or a mental health call. WADEPS allows users to easily compare data from different regions, including how many calls each law enforcement agency receives, how often they use force, and how often a person is injured because of that force.&nbsp;</p>
<p>The Legislature&nbsp;<a href="https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/ag-ferguson-bill-create-statewide-database-police-use-force-incidents-passes">passed a bill with bipartisan support in 2021</a> to create WADEPS. Lawmakers cited the need to collect and present data to the public to build community trust and improve transparency. WADEPS was developed through significant collaboration with law enforcement, community leaders, and criminal justice researchers.</p>
